title: Edgar Codd and the Relational Model (1970)
explainer: In June 1970, IBM researcher Edgar F. Codd published 'A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks' in Communications of the ACM, proposing that data be organized as simple tables of rows and columns related by shared values, instead of the rigid hierarchical or network structures common at the time. The paper's central goal was data independence: letting applications work with data without caring how it is physically stored, which is the same separation this lesson's tables and queries rest on. Codd's model was initially seen as mostly theoretical; it took most of the 1970s and 1980s for relational database products to become commercially dominant.

title: SEQUEL, SQL, and an Accidental Trademark Rename (Early 1970s)
explainer: Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce designed SEQUEL ('Structured English Query Language') at IBM in the early 1970s specifically to make Codd's relational model usable by people without a math or programming background - a deliberate design choice behind SQL's English-like syntax. The name was later shortened to SQL because 'SEQUEL' was already a trademark held by an unrelated company. Boyce, who also co-developed Boyce-Codd Normal Form, died suddenly in 1974, and the language continued developing within IBM's System R project before becoming the industry-standard query language.
